title: Date and time functions
summary_md: Current date, parts, formatting, arithmetic, differences, month/week boundaries, weekday numbering, parsing and half-open ranges, with MySQL and SQL Server compared argument by argument.

sections.heading: Current date and time
sections.body_md:
- MySQL: `CURDATE()` (date), `NOW()` / `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (datetime), `CURTIME()`, `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`. `NOW()` is fixed for the whole statement; `SYSDATE()` is evaluated per call.
- SQL Server: `GETDATE()` / `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (datetime), `SYSDATETIME()` (higher precision), `GETUTCDATE()`, and **no CURDATE**: today's date is `CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)`.
- Both return the **server's** clock and time zone. Anything built from them is non-deterministic - tests and examples should use fixed literals.
- 'Today' as a range, not a function on the column: `ts >= today AND ts < today + 1 day` (see the half-open ranges section).

syntax.tsql:
CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)   -- date
GETDATE()   /   SYSDATETIME()
GETUTCDATE()

examples.title: Rows before now
examples.explain_md: All 11 events are in the past, so the count is 11 whenever you run it. `NOW()` includes the time of day.
examples.mysql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS past_events FROM events WHERE event_ts < NOW();
examples.tsql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS past_events FROM events WHERE event_ts < GETDATE();

examples.title: Events today (half-open range)
examples.explain_md: Nothing in the sample data happened today, so 0. The pattern is the point: start of today inclusive, start of tomorrow exclusive.
examples.mysql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS events_today FROM events WHERE event_ts >= CURDATE() AND event_ts < CURDATE() + INTERVAL 1 DAY;
examples.tsql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS events_today FROM events WHERE event_ts >= CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) AND event_ts < DATEADD(DAY, 1, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE));

sections.heading: Extracting parts: YEAR, MONTH, EXTRACT, DATEPART, DATENAME
sections.body_md:
- `YEAR(d)`, `MONTH(d)`, `DAY(d)` exist in both engines and return integers.
- MySQL also has `QUARTER`, `HOUR`, `MINUTE`, `SECOND`, `DAYOFYEAR`, `MONTHNAME`, `DAYNAME`, `WEEK` and the standard `EXTRACT(unit FROM d)`.
- SQL Server has no EXTRACT/QUARTER: `DATEPART(part, d)` returns a number, `DATENAME(part, d)` returns text (`'March'`, `'Friday'`).
- `DATEPART` parts: `year, quarter, month, dayofyear, day, week, weekday, hour, minute, second`.
- Grouping by month: group by **both** `YEAR(d)` and `MONTH(d)`; grouping by `MONTH(d)` alone merges January 2023 with January 2024.

syntax.mysql:
YEAR(date) / MONTH(date) / DAY(date)
EXTRACT(unit FROM date)
DAYNAME(date) / MONTHNAME(date)
syntax.tsql:
YEAR(date) / MONTH(date) / DAY(date)
DATEPART(datepart, date)   -- number
DATENAME(datepart, date)   -- text

args.name: unit / datepart (position 1)
args.meaning: Which component: YEAR, QUARTER, MONTH, DAY, HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND ... (SQL Server also WEEKDAY, DAYOFYEAR, ISO_WEEK).

args.name: date (position 2)
args.meaning: The date, datetime or ISO-format string.

examples.title: Parts of 2024-03-15
examples.explain_md: 2024-03-15 is a Friday, the 75th day of the (leap) year, in quarter 1.
examples.mysql: SELECT YEAR(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS yr, MONTH(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS mo, DAY(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS dy, QUARTER(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS qtr, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS extract_mo, DAYOFYEAR(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS doy, MONTHNAME(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS month_name, DAYNAME(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS day_name;
examples.tsql: SELECT YEAR(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS yr, MONTH(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS mo, DAY(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS dy, DATEPART(QUARTER, CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS qtr, DATEPART(MONTH, CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS extract_mo, DATEPART(DAYOFYEAR, CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS doy, DATENAME(MONTH, CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS month_name, DATENAME(WEEKDAY, CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS day_name;

examples.title: Hour of day
examples.explain_md: Time parts work on DATETIME values. User 1's four events fall in hours 9 and 10.
examples.mysql: SELECT event_id, HOUR(event_ts) AS hr, MINUTE(event_ts) AS mi FROM events WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY event_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT event_id, DATEPART(HOUR, event_ts) AS hr, DATEPART(MINUTE, event_ts) AS mi FROM events WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY event_id;

examples.title: Completed revenue per month
examples.explain_md: Group by year and month, then order by the same two columns.
examples.mysql: SELECT YEAR(order_date) AS yr, MONTH(order_date) AS mo, COUNT(*) AS orders_n, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date) ORDER BY yr, mo;
examples.tsql: SELECT YEAR(order_date) AS yr, MONTH(order_date) AS mo, COUNT(*) AS orders_n, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date) ORDER BY yr, mo;

sections.heading: Formatting dates as text
sections.body_md:
- MySQL `DATE_FORMAT(date, format)` uses `%` specifiers. Year-month bucket: `DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m')`.
- SQL Server `FORMAT(date, 'yyyy-MM')` uses .NET patterns (slow and culture-aware; fine for reports, avoid on millions of rows). Fast alternative: `CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), d, 23)` for `yyyy-mm-dd`, or `LEFT(CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), d, 23), 7)` for `yyyy-mm`.
- Argument order: MySQL `(date, format)`, SQL Server `FORMAT(date, format)` and `CONVERT(type, date, style)`.
- Specifier case matters: MySQL `%m` month vs `%i` minutes; .NET `MM` month vs `mm` minutes, `HH` 24-hour vs `hh` 12-hour.
- A 'yyyy-MM' string sorts correctly; a month **name** (`%b`) sorts alphabetically - order by the numeric month.

- Full specifier table: see the **Specifier cheat sheet** example below.

syntax.tsql:
FORMAT(date, format [, culture])
CONVERT(VARCHAR(n), date, style)

args.name: date (position 1)
args.meaning: The date or datetime value (MySQL accepts date-like strings).

args.name: format (position 2)
args.meaning: MySQL: `%` specifiers. SQL Server FORMAT: .NET pattern.

examples.title: Specifier cheat sheet
examples.explain_md: Look-up table, not date math. Read across: the same meaning in MySQL `DATE_FORMAT`, SQL Server `FORMAT`, and the `CONVERT` style code where one exists.

tables.name: date_format_specifiers
tables.description_md: Cheat sheet: what to write for each date part. Column mysql_spec is for DATE_FORMAT/STR_TO_DATE, sqlserver_format for FORMAT, convert_style for CONVERT(VARCHAR, d, style).

examples.mysql: SELECT meaning, mysql_spec, sqlserver_format, convert_style FROM date_format_specifiers ORDER BY spec_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT meaning, mysql_spec, sqlserver_format, convert_style FROM date_format_specifiers ORDER BY spec_id;

examples.title: One timestamp, several formats
examples.explain_md: 2024-03-05 14:07:09 as year-month, a readable date, 24-hour time and weekday.
examples.mysql: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), '%Y-%m') AS ym, DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), '%b %e, %Y') AS pretty, DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), '%H:%i') AS hm, DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), '%W') AS weekday_name;
examples.tsql: SELECT FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), 'yyyy-MM') AS ym, FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), 'MMM d, yyyy') AS pretty, FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), 'HH:mm') AS hm, FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05 14:07:09' AS DATETIME), 'dddd') AS weekday_name;

examples.title: Month bucket from a date column
examples.explain_md: `'%Y-%m'` / `'yyyy-MM'` gives a sortable text key for monthly reports.
examples.mysql: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym, COUNT(*) AS orders_n FROM orders GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') ORDER BY ym;
examples.tsql: SELECT FORMAT(order_date, 'yyyy-MM') AS ym, COUNT(*) AS orders_n FROM orders GROUP BY FORMAT(order_date, 'yyyy-MM') ORDER BY ym;

examples.title: CONVERT styles
examples.explain_md: SQL Server's fast formatting: style 23 = `yyyy-mm-dd`, 112 = `yyyymmdd`, 101 = `mm/dd/yyyy`. MySQL equivalents use DATE_FORMAT.
examples.mysql: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), '%Y-%m-%d') AS iso, DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), '%Y%m%d') AS compact, DATE_FORMAT(CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), '%m/%d/%Y') AS us;
examples.tsql: SELECT CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), 23) AS iso, CONVERT(VARCHAR(8), CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), 112) AS compact, CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE), 101) AS us;

sections.heading: Adding and subtracting time
sections.body_md:
- MySQL: `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL n unit)`, `DATE_SUB(...)`, or the operator form `d + INTERVAL n unit` / `d - INTERVAL n unit`. Units: `SECOND, MINUTE, HOUR, DAY, WEEK, MONTH, QUARTER, YEAR`. `TIMESTAMPADD(unit, n, d)` also exists.
- SQL Server: `DATEADD(unit, n, d)`. Position 1 is the unit (`day`, `month`, `year`...), position 2 the signed amount, position 3 the date. Subtract with a negative `n`.
- **Month-end clamp**: adding a month to Jan 31 gives the last day of the next month (Feb 29 in 2024) in both engines. Adding a year to Feb 29 gives Feb 28.
- SQL Server `date + 1` works for DATETIME but **fails for DATE** - always use DATEADD. In MySQL `date + 1` is a number, not a date.
- 'Last 30 days': `d >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 30 DAY` / `d >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))`.

syntax.mysql:
DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit)
DATE_SUB(date, INTERVAL expr unit)
date + INTERVAL expr unit

args.name: expr / number
args.meaning: Signed amount to add. Negative subtracts.

args.name: unit / datepart
args.meaning: MySQL: after the INTERVAL amount. SQL Server: position 1.

examples.title: Month-end clamp
examples.explain_md: Jan 31 + 1 month lands on Feb 29; Feb 29 + 1 year lands on Feb 28; subtract with DATE_SUB or a negative DATEADD.
examples.mysql: SELECT DATE_ADD(CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE), INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS plus_month, DATE_ADD(CAST('2024-02-29' AS DATE), INTERVAL 1 YEAR) AS plus_year, DATE_SUB(CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE), INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS day_before, CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE) + INTERVAL 2 WEEK AS plus_2_weeks;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEADD(MONTH, 1, CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE)) AS plus_month, DATEADD(YEAR, 1, CAST('2024-02-29' AS DATE)) AS plus_year, DATEADD(DAY, -1, CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE)) AS day_before, DATEADD(WEEK, 2, CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE)) AS plus_2_weeks;

examples.title: Due date 30 days after the order
examples.explain_md: Operator form on a column.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_id, order_date, order_date + INTERVAL 30 DAY AS due_date FROM orders WHERE order_id <= 103 ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT order_id, order_date, DATEADD(DAY, 30, order_date) AS due_date FROM orders WHERE order_id <= 103 ORDER BY order_id;

sections.heading: Differences: DATEDIFF, TIMESTAMPDIFF
sections.body_md:
**The argument order flips between engines** - the top date-question slip.
- MySQL `DATEDIFF(end, start)` - **two arguments, result in days**, time of day ignored. `DATEDIFF('2024-03-01', '2024-02-01')` = 29. Reversed order gives a negative number.
- SQL Server `DATEDIFF(unit, start, end)` - **three arguments**: position 1 the unit, then start, then end. Same 29 days, written `DATEDIFF(DAY, '2024-02-01', '2024-03-01')`.
- MySQL `TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, start, end)` takes the unit first like SQL Server and returns **complete units** (floors the elapsed time).
- SQL Server `DATEDIFF` counts **boundaries crossed**, not elapsed time: `DATEDIFF(YEAR, '2023-12-31', '2024-01-01')` = 1 and `DATEDIFF(MONTH, '2024-01-31', '2024-02-01')` = 1, although one day passed. The same pair gives 0 in MySQL `TIMESTAMPDIFF`.
- Full months in SQL Server: `DATEDIFF(MONTH, s, e) - CASE WHEN DAY(e) < DAY(s) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END`.
- Inclusive day count (both endpoints): add 1.
- SQL Server `DATEDIFF` returns INT; use `DATEDIFF_BIG` for seconds over ~68 years.

syntax.mysql:
DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date)           -- days
TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, start, end)       -- whole units

args.name: end (MySQL DATEDIFF position 1)
args.meaning: The later date; the result is positive when this is later.

args.name: unit / datepart (TIMESTAMPDIFF and SQL Server DATEDIFF position 1)
args.meaning: SECOND, MINUTE, HOUR, DAY, WEEK, MONTH, QUARTER, YEAR.

args.name: start, end (positions 2 and 3)
args.meaning: Order is (start, end) in both TIMESTAMPDIFF and SQL Server DATEDIFF.

examples.title: Days between dates, both orders
examples.explain_md: Feb 2024 has 29 days. MySQL takes (end, start); SQL Server takes (unit, start, end). Swapping the dates negates the answer.
examples.mysql: SELECT DATEDIFF(CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE), CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) AS days_forward, DATEDIFF(CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE)) AS days_reversed;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEDIFF(DAY, CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE)) AS days_forward, DATEDIFF(DAY, CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE), CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) AS days_reversed;

examples.title: Complete months
examples.explain_md: Jan 31 to Feb 1 is 0 full months, Jan 15 to Mar 14 is 1, Jan 15 to Mar 15 is 2.
examples.mysql: SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) AS m_a, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-14' AS DATE)) AS m_b, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS m_c;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DAY(CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) < DAY(CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m_a, DATEDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-14' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DAY(CAST('2024-03-14' AS DATE)) < DAY(CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m_b, DATEDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DAY(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) < DAY(CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m_c;
examples.dialect_note_md: The T-SQL subtracts 1 when the end day-of-month is earlier than the start day, turning boundary counts into complete months.

examples.title: Boundary counting vs elapsed time
examples.explain_md: One day apart, but the year boundary was crossed.
examples.mysql: SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)) AS years_diff, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)) AS months_diff, DATEDIFF(CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE), CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE)) AS days_diff;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEDIFF(YEAR, CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)) AS years_diff, DATEDIFF(MONTH, CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)) AS months_diff, DATEDIFF(DAY, CAST('2023-12-31' AS DATE), CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)) AS days_diff;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server returns 1, 1, 1 (a year and a month boundary are crossed); MySQL TIMESTAMPDIFF returns 0, 0 and DATEDIFF returns 1. This is a genuine semantic difference.

examples.title: Minutes between consecutive events
examples.explain_md: User 1's gaps: first event has no predecessor (NULL), then 10, 45 and 10 minutes. `LAG` fetches the previous timestamp.
examples.mysql: SELECT event_id, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id), event_ts) AS gap_min FROM events WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY event_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT event_id, DATEDIFF(MINUTE, LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id), event_ts) AS gap_min FROM events WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY event_id;

pitfalls_md: MySQL DATEDIFF ignores the time part: `DATEDIFF('2024-01-02 00:01', '2024-01-01 23:59')` is 1 although 2 minutes passed.
SQL Server `DATEDIFF(DAY, ...)` on DATETIME values also counts midnight crossings, not 24-hour periods.

sections.heading: Start/end of month, week, year
sections.body_md:
- **First day of month**: MySQL `d - INTERVAL (DAY(d) - 1) DAY` (stays a DATE). `DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m-01')` returns text. SQL Server: `DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), MONTH(d), 1)`; **2022+** `DATETRUNC(MONTH, d)`; classic `DATEADD(MONTH, DATEDIFF(MONTH, 0, d), 0)`.
- **Last day of month**: MySQL `LAST_DAY(d)`; SQL Server `EOMONTH(d [, months_to_add])`. `EOMONTH(d, -1)` is the end of the previous month; add 1 day to get this month's start.
- **First of year**: MySQL `MAKEDATE(YEAR(d), 1)`; SQL Server `DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), 1, 1)`.
- **Week start**: MySQL Monday: `d - INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY`; Sunday: `d - INTERVAL (DAYOFWEEK(d) - 1) DAY`. SQL Server Monday (default DATEFIRST): `DATEADD(DAY, -((DATEPART(WEEKDAY, d) + 5) % 7), d)`; 2022+ `DATETRUNC(ISO_WEEK, d)` is Monday, while `DATETRUNC(WEEK, d)` depends on `SET DATEFIRST`.
- Month length: `DAY(LAST_DAY(d))` / `DAY(EOMONTH(d))`.
- Bucketing to month: group by the first-of-month DATE, not by text, so ordering and joins stay simple.

syntax.mysql:
LAST_DAY(date)
MAKEDATE(year, dayofyear)
date - INTERVAL (DAY(date) - 1) DAY
syntax.tsql:
EOMONTH(date [, months_to_add])
DATEFROMPARTS(year, month, day)
DATETRUNC(datepart, date)   -- 2022+

args.name: months_to_add (EOMONTH position 2)
args.meaning: Optional signed month offset applied before taking the month end.

examples.title: First day and last day of the month
examples.explain_md: Feb 2024 is a leap February, so the last day is the 29th; the month has 29 days.
examples.mysql: SELECT CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE) - INTERVAL (DAY(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE)) - 1) DAY AS month_start, LAST_DAY(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE)) AS month_end, DAY(LAST_DAY(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE))) AS days_in_month, LAST_DAY(CAST('2023-02-10' AS DATE)) AS month_end_2023;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE)), MONTH(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE)), 1) AS month_start, EOMONTH(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE)) AS month_end, DAY(EOMONTH(CAST('2024-02-10' AS DATE))) AS days_in_month, EOMONTH(CAST('2023-02-10' AS DATE)) AS month_end_2023;

examples.title: Group orders by first-of-month
examples.explain_md: A real DATE bucket sorts and joins naturally. Completed orders only.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_date - INTERVAL (DAY(order_date) - 1) DAY AS month_start, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY order_date - INTERVAL (DAY(order_date) - 1) DAY ORDER BY month_start;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1) AS month_start, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1) ORDER BY month_start;

examples.title: Monday of the week
examples.explain_md: 2024-03-06 is a Wednesday; its ISO week starts Monday 2024-03-04. MySQL WEEKDAY is 0 for Monday.
examples.mysql: SELECT CAST('2024-03-06' AS DATE) - INTERVAL WEEKDAY(CAST('2024-03-06' AS DATE)) DAY AS week_start_monday;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEADD(DAY, -((DATEPART(WEEKDAY, CAST('2024-03-06' AS DATE)) + 5) % 7), CAST('2024-03-06' AS DATE)) AS week_start_monday;
examples.dialect_note_md: Assumes the default `DATEFIRST 7` (Sunday = 1). On SQL Server 2022+ the setting-proof form is `DATETRUNC(ISO_WEEK, d)`. A DATEFIRST-independent classic: `DATEADD(DAY, DATEDIFF(DAY, '1900-01-01', d) / 7 * 7, '1900-01-01')` (1900-01-01 was a Monday).

sections.heading: Day of week numbering
sections.body_md:
Three numbering schemes - memorise which engine uses which.
- MySQL `DAYOFWEEK(d)`: **1 = Sunday** ... 7 = Saturday. MySQL `WEEKDAY(d)`: **0 = Monday** ... 6 = Sunday. `DAYNAME(d)` gives the name.
- SQL Server `DATEPART(WEEKDAY, d)`: depends on `SET DATEFIRST` (default 7 for US English, which makes **1 = Sunday**, like DAYOFWEEK). With `DATEFIRST 1` Monday is 1. Language settings change it too.
- Locale-proof SQL Server tests: `DATENAME(WEEKDAY, d)` (language-dependent text) or `(DATEPART(WEEKDAY, d) + @@DATEFIRST) % 7` which is 0 for Saturday and 1 for Sunday regardless of DATEFIRST.
- ISO week number: MySQL `WEEK(d, 3)` / `WEEKOFYEAR(d)`; SQL Server `DATEPART(ISO_WEEK, d)`. Plain `WEEK(d)` (mode 0) and `DATEPART(WEEK, d)` follow Sunday-first rules and differ around New Year.
- Weekend filter in MySQL: `DAYOFWEEK(d) IN (1, 7)` (or `WEEKDAY(d) >= 5`).

syntax.tsql:
DATEPART(WEEKDAY, date)   -- depends on DATEFIRST
DATENAME(WEEKDAY, date)   -- text

examples.title: One week of numbers
examples.explain_md: 2024-03-01 is a Friday: DAYOFWEEK 6 (Sunday = 1), WEEKDAY 4 (Monday = 0).
examples.mysql: SELECT sale_date, DAYNAME(sale_date) AS day_name, DAYOFWEEK(sale_date) AS dayofweek_sun1, WEEKDAY(sale_date) AS weekday_mon0 FROM daily_sales WHERE region = 'East' AND sale_date <= '2024-03-04' ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql: SELECT sale_date, DATENAME(WEEKDAY, sale_date) AS day_name, DATEPART(WEEKDAY, sale_date) AS dayofweek_sun1, (DATEPART(WEEKDAY, sale_date) + 5) % 7 AS weekday_mon0 FROM daily_sales WHERE region = 'East' AND sale_date <= '2024-03-04' ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.dialect_note_md: The SQL Server numbers assume the default `DATEFIRST 7` (Sunday = 1); `(DATEPART(WEEKDAY, d) + 5) % 7` converts that to Monday = 0.

examples.title: Weekend vs weekday revenue
examples.explain_md: Mar 2-3 and 9-10 are weekends. Totals across both regions.
examples.mysql: SELECT CASE WHEN DAYOFWEEK(sale_date) IN (1, 7) THEN 'weekend' ELSE 'weekday' END AS day_type, SUM(revenue) AS revenue FROM daily_sales GROUP BY CASE WHEN DAYOFWEEK(sale_date) IN (1, 7) THEN 'weekend' ELSE 'weekday' END ORDER BY day_type;
examples.tsql: SELECT CASE WHEN DATEPART(WEEKDAY, sale_date) IN (1, 7) THEN 'weekend' ELSE 'weekday' END AS day_type, SUM(revenue) AS revenue FROM daily_sales GROUP BY CASE WHEN DATEPART(WEEKDAY, sale_date) IN (1, 7) THEN 'weekend' ELSE 'weekday' END ORDER BY day_type;
examples.dialect_note_md: Correct only when `DATEFIRST` is 7 (the US English default). For a setting-proof test use `DATENAME(WEEKDAY, d) IN ('Saturday', 'Sunday')` or the `@@DATEFIRST` formula.

sections.heading: Parsing text into dates
sections.body_md:
- ISO text `'YYYY-MM-DD'` converts with `CAST(s AS DATE)` in both engines. Anything else needs a format.
- MySQL `STR_TO_DATE(str, format)` with the same `%` specifiers as DATE_FORMAT. Position 1 = the text, position 2 = its format. Returns NULL (with a warning) for text that does not match; use `%d/%m/%Y` for day-first.
- SQL Server `CONVERT(DATE, str, style)`: position 1 the target type, 2 the text, 3 the style code of the **input** (103 = `dd/mm/yyyy`, 101 = `mm/dd/yyyy`, 112 = `yyyymmdd`). `TRY_CONVERT` returns NULL on failure where CONVERT raises an error. `PARSE(str AS DATE USING 'en-GB')` is culture-based and slow.
- `yyyymmdd` (no dashes) is the one text form SQL Server always reads correctly, regardless of `SET LANGUAGE` / `DATEFORMAT`. For DATETIME (not DATETIME2/DATE), `'2024-03-05'` can be read as year-day-month in some languages.
- Manual parse when nothing else works: `DATEFROMPARTS(CAST(SUBSTRING(s, 7, 4) AS INT), CAST(SUBSTRING(s, 4, 2) AS INT), CAST(LEFT(s, 2) AS INT))` for `'dd/mm/yyyy'`.

syntax.tsql:
CONVERT(DATE, str [, style])
TRY_CONVERT(DATE, str [, style])
TRY_CAST(str AS DATE)

args.name: format (position 2)
args.meaning: MySQL `%` layout describing the text exactly, e.g. `%d/%m/%Y`, `%M %e, %Y`.

args.name: style (CONVERT position 3)
args.meaning: Numeric code for the input layout: 101 mm/dd/yyyy, 103 dd/mm/yyyy, 104 dd.mm.yyyy, 112 yyyymmdd, 23 yyyy-mm-dd.

examples.title: ISO text to DATE
examples.explain_md: The ISO form needs no format string; CAST handles it in both engines.
examples.mysql: SELECT CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE) AS parsed, CAST('2024-03-15 08:30:00' AS DATETIME) AS parsed_ts, YEAR(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS yr;
examples.tsql: SELECT CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE) AS parsed, CAST('2024-03-15 08:30:00' AS DATETIME) AS parsed_ts, YEAR(CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)) AS yr;

examples.title: Day-first text
examples.explain_md: MySQL names the layout with a format; the T-SQL below slices the pieces so it runs everywhere (`CONVERT(DATE, '15/03/2024', 103)` is the shorthand).
examples.mysql: SELECT STR_TO_DATE('15/03/2024', '%d/%m/%Y') AS parsed_dmy, STR_TO_DATE('2024-03-05', '%Y-%m-%d') AS parsed_iso;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(CAST(SUBSTRING('15/03/2024', 7, 4) AS INT), CAST(SUBSTRING('15/03/2024', 4, 2) AS INT), CAST(LEFT('15/03/2024', 2) AS INT)) AS parsed_dmy, CAST('2024-03-05' AS DATE) AS parsed_iso;
examples.dialect_note_md: In SQL Server write `CONVERT(DATE, '15/03/2024', 103)`; the slicing form above is only used so the example also runs in the browser.

sections.heading: Half-open ranges: all of a day or a month
sections.body_md:
Use `>= start AND < next_start`. It is correct for DATE, DATETIME and fractional seconds, and it can use an index.
- Whole day: `ts >= '2024-05-01' AND ts < '2024-05-02'` (or `< d + INTERVAL 1 DAY`).
- Whole month: `d >= '2024-02-01' AND d < '2024-03-01'`, with the end computed as `start + INTERVAL 1 MONTH` / `DATEADD(MONTH, 1, start)`.
- `BETWEEN '2024-05-01' AND '2024-05-01'` on a DATETIME means midnight to midnight: it misses everything after 00:00:00. `BETWEEN a AND '2024-05-31 23:59:59'` still drops the last second's fractions.
- `BETWEEN` is fine on DATE columns (inclusive both ends, no time part).
- Do not wrap the column: `WHERE YEAR(d) = 2024` or `DATE(ts) = '2024-05-01'` forces a scan; compare the raw column against a range.

examples.title: All events on 2024-05-01
examples.explain_md: The half-open range finds all 7 events of that day (user 3 at 18:00 included); the BETWEEN version finds none because every event has a time after midnight.
examples.mysql: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_ts >= '2024-05-01' AND event_ts < '2024-05-02') AS half_open, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_ts BETWEEN '2024-05-01' AND '2024-05-01') AS between_trap;
examples.tsql: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_ts >= '2024-05-01' AND event_ts < '2024-05-02') AS half_open, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_ts BETWEEN '2024-05-01' AND '2024-05-01') AS between_trap;

examples.title: Orders placed in February 2024
examples.explain_md: Start inclusive, next month's start exclusive; orders 103-106.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_date >= CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE) AND order_date < CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE) + INTERVAL 1 MONTH ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_date >= CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE) AND order_date < DATEADD(MONTH, 1, CAST('2024-02-01' AS DATE)) ORDER BY order_id;

pitfalls_md: Months have different lengths: derive the end from the start (`start + 1 MONTH`) instead of hard-coding the 30th or 31st.
SQL Server: write date literals as `'YYYYMMDD'` or `'YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss'` when comparing to DATETIME so `SET DATEFORMAT` cannot change the meaning.

sections.heading: Age and tenure
sections.body_md:
'How many full years has this person been here?' needs complete-unit counting.
- MySQL: `TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, start, ref)` is already complete years (anniversary-aware). `TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, ...)` likewise.
- SQL Server: `DATEDIFF(YEAR, start, ref)` only counts calendar-year boundaries, so subtract 1 if the anniversary has not happened yet: `DATEDIFF(YEAR, s, ref) - CASE WHEN DATEADD(YEAR, DATEDIFF(YEAR, s, ref), s) > ref THEN 1 ELSE 0 END`.
- Never `DATEDIFF(DAY, ...) / 365`: leap years drift.
- Use a **fixed reference date** in reports and tests (`'2024-12-31'`), or pass `CURDATE()` / `GETDATE()` in production.
- Days of tenure: MySQL `DATEDIFF(ref, hire)`; SQL Server `DATEDIFF(DAY, hire, ref)`.

examples.title: Complete years and months on 2024-12-31
examples.explain_md: Dev joined 2021-05-03: 3 full years, 43 full months. Hal joined 2024-01-08: 0 years, 11 months.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, hire_date, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) AS full_years, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) AS full_months, DATEDIFF(CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE), hire_date) AS days FROM employees WHERE emp_id IN (4, 8, 10) ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, hire_date, DATEDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DATEADD(YEAR, DATEDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)), hire_date) > CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS full_years, DATEDIFF(MONTH, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DAY(CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) < DAY(hire_date) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS full_months, DATEDIFF(DAY, hire_date, CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)) AS days FROM employees WHERE emp_id IN (4, 8, 10) ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Age with a birthday not yet reached
examples.explain_md: Born 1990-09-15, on 2024-06-01: calendar years differ by 34 but the person is 33.
examples.mysql: SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-06-01' AS DATE)) AS age_years, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-09-15' AS DATE)) AS age_on_birthday;
examples.tsql: SELECT DATEDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-06-01' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DATEADD(YEAR, DATEDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-06-01' AS DATE)), CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE)) > CAST('2024-06-01' AS DATE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS age_years, DATEDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-09-15' AS DATE)) - CASE WHEN DATEADD(YEAR, DATEDIFF(YEAR, CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE), CAST('2024-09-15' AS DATE)), CAST('1990-09-15' AS DATE)) > CAST('2024-09-15' AS DATE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS age_on_birthday;

pitfalls_md: Feb 29 birthdays: `DATEADD(YEAR, n, '2000-02-29')` returns Feb 28 in non-leap years, so such people age one day early under the DATEADD idiom.
